(1) The provided government sources (the 2015 civic edition of the resuscitation guideline and the Fire and Disaster Management Agency (FDMA) survival handbook) never define a simple fracture, and never separate it from a crack (an incomplete fracture). The statement cannot be confirmed from a primary source.

(2) The FDMA handbook p.37 only lists signs of a fracture, such as swelling or deformity and bone ends that feel displaced. Neither source says whether grating sounds (軋轢音) or deformity belong to complete or to incomplete fractures. This cannot be confirmed.

(3) The guideline p.51 (PDF p.60) says to immobilise a deformed limb and that it does not need to be returned to its original shape. The handbook p.37 says to fix the fractured part firmly and not move it. Both contradict 'move it well to judge the extent', so this choice is confirmed as false.

(4) The handbook p.37 says 'make it longer than the joints above and below the fracture', which supports the length requirement. The 'wide' requirement (幅の広いもの) is not stated in either source, so only part of the statement is confirmed.

(5) Neither source says whether a suspected spinal-cord injury should or should not be carried on a hard board. The guideline p.51-52 (PDF p.60-61) only says to hold the head with both hands and keep the neck still. This cannot be confirmed.

(1) Slide 1 of the MHLW food-poisoning classification material lists Campylobacter jejuni/coli as an infection-type bacterium, and lists Clostridium botulinum and Staphylococcus aureus as toxin-type. So calling Campylobacter an example of toxin-type poisoning is confirmed false.
(2) The source only classifies C. botulinum as a food-borne toxin type. Nothing in the provided sources says its toxin is a neurotoxin, so this cannot be confirmed.
(3) The source only classifies S. aureus as a food-borne toxin type. Nothing in the provided sources says its toxin is heat-stable, so this cannot be confirmed.

(4) The source only lists Vibrio parahaemolyticus as an infection-type bacterium. Nothing in the provided sources gives the alternative name 'pathogenic halophilic bacterium' (病原性好塩菌), so this cannot be confirmed.

(5) The MHLW norovirus Q&A says norovirus is fully inactivated by sodium hypochlorite, chlorous acid water or heat, and that heating in hot water at 85 °C or above for at least 1 minute is effective. This supports the choice.

The classification material is an old 2007 information-session handout (its data runs to H18, i.e. 2006). The classification it states is basic and does not change, so this does not block applicability.
